fieldworkDocument.title: Measgaichte / Miscellaneous
fieldworkDocument.note: [NOTES: in IPA transcriptions, the fieldworker uses [w] for [ɯ].]

item.description: [ku̜rəhu̜ɫuxĩnʹ] Note: the stick jutting up from the thatch at the end of a blackhouse (màs an tighe).
Note: the stick jutting up from the thatch at the end of a blackhouse (ceann an tighe).
[t̪w:vɑṉ] Note: the horizontal spars lying across the ties on a blackhouse roof.
[ˈklɛ] Note: the sticks laid on top of the “taobhain” [q.v.] on a blackhouse roof. Running from the top of the wall to the ridge-pole.
Note: described as the point at which the “ceangail” and the top of the wall come together. (Usually described as being two or three feet up from the wall.)
[t̪oɫˈɔd̪ɑ̃nʹ] Note: exit at “màs an tighe” to allow passage of cattle urine and any other seepage.
[lʹɛkheʃəɾɑx] Note: pl. [lʹɛkəṉʃeʃəɾɑx]. Flat stones put under the cattle to prevent them from getting stuck in the manure. (At a time when earth wasn’t allowed to be taken in to put under them.)
[dʹil] Note: a covered drain under the floor of the blackhouse.
[kɑlɑv] Note: partition between the “àite-teine” and the “cùlaist”.
[lʹɛkˈu̟ɾɑɫɑx] Note: an upright stone just inside the front door, between it and the door leading to the living quarters to direct cattle to go their own way.
Quot.: “toll an t-sobhail” also “darus toll an t-sobhail”. Note: an opening on the far side of the barn from the main house, about three feet high. Built up with stones. To prevent stealing.
[ɫɑ̃:xɾɑṉ] Note: flail handle.
Note: flail striker.
Note: thong of softened sheepskin tying the “buailtean” [q.v.] to the “làmhchran” [q.v.].
Quot.: “calg air an eòrna”. Note: barley chaff.
Quot.: sgalpan air a’ choirc. Note: corn chaff (oats).
Note: a short-(rounded) stick for threshing a sheaf, the sheaf being held under one arm and the shock struck with the stick.
[mɔ̃ĩlʹɑṉ] Quot.: “moighlean fodair”. Note: a bundle of straw.
Quot.: a’ cheallach. Note: the fireplace in a grain kiln.
[ˈst̪ɾɛ̃ıɡ] Note: the covering of straw on which the seed was put for drying in the kiln.
[d̪ɾɔvɑlʹtʹ] Note: mill hopper. Made of straw-rope (sioman connlaich).
Note: wooden box under the hopper in a mill.

Note: a stick attached at one end to the “bròg” [q.v.] in a grinding mill. The other end lay on the upper grindstone. As the stone turned it caused the “bròg” to vibrate, thus releasing the seed gradually into the “sùil” [q.v.].
Quot.: “sùil na muinnle”. Note: the centre hole in the top millstone.
Note: the stick attached to the lower mill-stone and coming up through the centre hole of the top mill-stone.
Quot.: “an t-sail-aotrom”. Note: this regulated the coarseness of the meal by adjusting the clearance between the two mill-stones.
Quot.: “a’ roth as an toll-làir”. Note: where the water wheel of the mill was situated.
[lʹıɤ] Note: pl. [lʹıɤhəṉ]. The mill-wheel blades.
Note: grass growing again among corn stubble after the corn has been scythed.
Note: a small cultivable patch of land, perhaps surrounded by stones. (Arnol very stony.)
Note: a bigger area of cultivable ground, perhaps three times as big as a “ceann” [q.v.]. Tends to be square.
Note: small cultivable patch with a ditch on each side of it.
[lʹo:b] Note: a longer piece of ground than a “clàr” [q.v.] but as broad. Tends to be oblong.
[ɑfəɫ] Quot.: “afall càil”. Note: a small walled garden in which “planntraisean” were planted. “Leas bheag”.
Quot.: “sgrìob feòir”, “sgrìob coirce”. Note: a swathe.
Quot.: “bad coirc”. Note: sheaf of oats.
Quot.: beum eòrna. Note: sheaf of barley.
Quot.: “adag coirc”. Note: stook of oats (12 sheaves).
[bɫɑi] Quot.: bloigh eòrna. Note: row of standing sheaves with their heads bent over.
Quot.: tòrr coirc. Note: hut of corn.
Quot.: curruchdag eòrna. Note: hut of barley (comprising 3 “bloighean” [q.v.]).
Quot.: sìg feòir. Note: loaf-shaped haystack.
Quot.: goc feòir. Note: haycock.

Quot.: “am beum dubh”. Note: nuair a bhiodh iad a’ deanamh cruach eòrna bhiodh iad a’ cur na beumannan a bha air an sgathadh [q.v.] do’n mheadhoin agus na beumannan dubh a muigh. Barley pulled up by the roots.
Quot.: a’ sgathadh an eòrna. Note: cutting the barley sheaves to remove the lower part (with the roots for thatching).
Quot.: an easlainte-cham. Note: disease in cattle and sheep causing a twist in the neck.
Quot.: a’ chródaich [xɾo:d̪iç] (not nasal). Note: illness said to be in sheep. They weakened at the “knees” and went about on them. Front legs.
Quot.: an tuathallan. Note: illness in sheep caused by water sac on the brain.
[d̪ɤlʹə] Quot.: an doille. Note: blindness in sheep, “sgleò a’ tighinn air na sùilean aca”.
[bu̜ɤɫt̪ɑx] Quot.: “Bhiodh i bualtach air an doille a thighinn oirre.” Note: We say [bu̟ɤlʹtʹɑx].
Quot.: an illness which affected cattle. Thinks it was fits, but not sure. Cure: “Bha sioman connlach air fhighe ceàrr air a chur timchioll air druim agus mionach a’ bheathaich”.

Quot.: “an tinneas-air-ais”. Note: epilepsy. Cure: a black cock with no white feathers was killed and buried at the spot where the fits had first taken place. The patient then had to sleep there for one night.
[kɫɑ̃ĩf] Quot.: a’ chlaimh. Note: sheep scab.
Note: smearing of sheep with a mixture of tar and, usually, dogfish oil.
[pȷɑ:ʴḏ] Note: strip of wool coming from the cards. [NOTES: the turned r used for the symbol which is unclear in the original.]
[rɛhɑṉ] Note: roller on spinning-wheel, round which the band from the big wheel went.
[dʹel] Note: spindle in spinning-wheel.
Note: foot-board of the spinning-wheel.
Quot.: na maighdeannan. Note: uprights on spinning-wheel supporting the flyer.
Note: the post(s) in the byre to which a cow was tied.
[smɛ̃ɑɡ] Note: the portion of the cow’s tether round its neck when tied inside.
[ku̜:ɫɑkĩnʹ] Note: the part of the cow’s tether attaching the “smeadhag” [q.v.] to the “stiall” [q.v.] when tied inside.
[kɔt̪ɑṉ] Note: small turf enclosure for a young calf at the shieling. Usually built into a bank and enclosed with turf divots.
Note: upright stone at a shieling for cows to scratch themselves.

[d̪ɑɾəsˈiɤt̪] Note: there were two openings on the older type of shieling, one completely open and the other closed up with turf divots. It depended on the direction of the wind which one was open and which one was shut. The divots would be shifted from one to the other. The “darus-iadht” was the closed one.

[ĩməðiç] Quot.: “Na chuir sibh a mach an imrich fhathast?” “An d’thug sibh dhachaidh an imrich fhathast.” Note: the clothing, utensils, etc. which were taken to the shieling at the beginning of summer and brought back at the end of the season.
[ˈĩmidʹəɫ] Note: piece of sheepskin stretched over the mouth of a milk-pail and secured with a string outside the rim.
[kɔrɔhən̪ɑṉ] Note: wooden swivel device used in the tethering of sheep.
[kɔsɡɑɾəɣ] Note: souming.
[ɡʹibɑɡ] gibeag fraoich. Note: small bundle of heather.
[cɤ̃ũ̟bəɫ] Quot.: ciomball fraoich. Note: large bundle of heather.
[ʃıɔɫvõɫ] Note: used for chaff as well as “sgalpan” [q.v.], “calg” [q.v.].
[sɡʹɑp] Note: bag of woven straw, slung at one’s side, for cuddy-fishing.
[cwsɑṉ] Note: fairly shallow vessel like a basin, made of straw. Had perpendicular sides.
[ʃec] Note: a large bag, made of woven straw, used for taking grain to the kiln. Carried on the back with a rope round it and round the chest. Held about quantity of two ordinary bags.
[ɫu̜:ɑɡ] Note: a piece of rope tightened just above the joint on one of the hind legs of a sheep. Prevented it from running.
Note: seen most often on lambs. A rope tied between one hind leg and one front leg.
[ˈdʹeən̪] Note: rope tied between two front legs of a horse. Prevented it from running.
Note: a cloud formation usually above the horizon. Strips of cloud coming together at one focal point. Could expect rain from this direction.
[ʃlʹɤ̃ĩnʹtʹɑx] Note: very wet snowflakes, disappearing on contact with the ground.
[flw̃ṉ] Quot.: “Flion shneachd”. Note: understood by him as very fine powdery snow.
[kɑfəɣɫɑ:ɾ] Note: drifting snow.

Note: emphasis on “fuar”. Can be seen sometimes in the very early morning on grass and potato leaves. Says it was colder than the usual dew and if it wasn’t away before the sun rose, “bhiodh am feur agus duilleagan a’ bhuntàta air an losgadh”.
[ʃĩɤ̃ṉ] Note: very fine, drizzly rain.
[ˈcu̟həɾɑṉiç] Note: very fine, drizzly rain.
[ɫũ̜nʹ] Note: according to N.C. seen on a very hot day in the one spot, perhaps only 100 yards away. A visual disturbance in the air often accompanied by a whirlwind.
Note: whirlwind.
Note: short heavy shower.
Note: heavy shower of medium length.
Note: foamy sea.
Quot.: siaban na mara. Note: says it was blown foam, forming a sort of “ceò”.
[kɑfəɣmɑɾə] Note: spindrift, much heavier than “siaban” [q.v.], according to N.C.
[kɑlʹəbĩɤ̃ṉɑṉ] Note: phosphorescence as seen on fish hanging in the house or salted in a tub.
[spɾu̟l] Note: “l” lengthened as in “fool”. Name given to the lead (about 6"-7" long) in a “dorgh”.
Note: square frame on which fishing line is wound.
Note: when fishing for dogfish, herring or mackerel bait was used until a dogfish was caught. Then the “caolan-dubh” was removed from it and bits of it used for bait after that.
[t̪u̟:k] Note: bung in a boat.
[fɑɫɑməd̪ɑð] Note: tiller.
[sɔ:ɫə] Note: piece of flooring in a boat.
[kɾɑ̃ɡ] Note: thole-pin.
Quot.: an traigh [sic] fheamad. Note: (Put also under feamainn.)
[ɫɑ̃ĩɡʹɑð] Quot.: laingear Bhràgair, laingear Arnol, laingear Bharabhais. Note: understood as being the area uncovered at low tide, where shellfish were collected, etc.
Note: large hollows in the shingle into which the seaweed coming ashore was put. Manure was taken to it by creel in the spring time. The mixture used on the ground. Sandy soil needed this.
Quot.: putan buntàta. Note: small patches of potatoes planted, e.g. between boulders or cairns.
[t̪on̪ɑɡ] Quot.: tonnag langainn. Note: small fish found inshore – probably the young ling. Got under stones at very low tide.
Note: a large hand-net for saithe-fishing.
[pɾɔ̃n̪ɔvw̃sɡ] Note: bait, such as mashed potatoes or bits of dogfish, thrown on the water to attract saithe (cuddies, etc.)
[lʹiɑɡ] Note: scum, e.g. on water.
[t̪oˈɫɛx] Note: the opening at the end of a byre to allow a horse and cart to back in for manure.
[ɡʹwd̪ɾəmɑṉ] Note: a frolicsome, giddy person.
[cıɾcɑṉ] Note: applied to a misbehaving boy.
[pɾiɡɑṉ] Note: “Duine a bhiodh dona gu buaireadh.”
[ɡɾı:ləbɑṉ] Note: small person, child or adult.
[spɾɔkəðə] Note: a person full of aggressive self-importance. Adj. sprocach.
Note: a very light warm shower of rain falling with the sun out at the same time.
[sɡu̟tʹə] Quot.: (1) a’ sguite thoisich. (2) a’ sguite dheiridh. Note: (1) stempost. (2) sternpost.
Note: gunwale.
Quot.: crotaichean ràimh. Note: pieces of wood put on an oar to prevent it from chafing where it lies between the thole-pins.
Note: a gaff.
[lʹı:ɑx] Note: oily.
[lʹıɑɡɑx] Quot.: “rud leugach”. Note: something with scum left on it.
[u̟:lʹəṉ] Note: globules of oil on the surface of a liquid.
[ɑxəd̪u̟] Quot.: “Thàinig an t-achadh-dubh.” Note: the reappearance of the ground after the snow melts.
[smõkɑṉ] Note: mixture of fine, red seaweed washed ashore.
[smȷɑ̃ʴsṯɑṉ] Note: curly seaweed. [NOTES: the turned r used for the symbol which is unclear in the original.]
[ɫɑ̃ŋɡəd̪ɑð] Note: kind of tangle in the form of long, oily strips attached to the “duibhean”, a type of “stamh”.
Note: type of tangle, not as long as “langadair” [q.v.], but broader.
[mĩɾcɑṉ] Note: alaria esculenta.
[dʹu̜ɫu̜x] Note: growths on the stem of the “mircean” [q.v.] at the base of the leaf.
[sɫɑu̟kɑṉ] Note: fine type of seaweed scraped from rocks. Boiled and eaten. Eaten by invalids. Akin to “duileasg” but finer.
[kɑrɑçɡʹɑṉ] Note: the lump at the base of tangle, attaching it to the rock.
[fıɑɫɔx] Note: waterlogged area with grass growing in it.
Note: coarse grass growing in wet places.
[bɾĩɑ̃ɫɑx] Note: soft, water-logged area.
Quot.: frith-rathad nan caorach. Note: sheep-track on the moor.
Note: stepping-stones across a burn.
Quot.: tullach na h-àirigh.
[spɤ̃ŋɡɑdʹ] Note: a sling.
[st̪ɾı:lıɡʹɑṉ] Note: a hoop rolled along the ground.
Quot.: “Strìlig e.” Note: Roll it.
[t̪u̟d̪əɫɑṉṉəhɑ:hi] Note: Blind Man’s Buff.
Quot.: “brùchd feamainn”. Note: heap of seaweed washed ashore.
[su̟liçɑɡ] Note: large rounded stone on the shore (clach-mhuile).
Note: about two weeks of good weather in November.
[kɤlʹɑɡ] Note: shinty ball.
[tɤıli] Quot.: Chuir iad tuidhlidh oirnn. Note: goal in shinty.
Quot.: Seas do [huɫıçəṉ]. Note: said by one player in a shinty side to an opposing player, demanding him to take a proper stance with his stick.
[ɤ̃ĩlʹɑɡ] Note: elbow jab.
[t̪ɤıu̟ɤɾɑx] Note: an additional room for sleeping, opening sometimes from the living room (aite-teine), sometimes from the “culaist”.
Note: toy which made a whirring noise.
Note: water blackened by soot falling from a blackhouse roof.
Note: straw from thatch coming down between the “cabair” and being covered with soot. (?)
Note: water coming up through the floor of a blackhouse due to very heavy rain running down the walls.
Note: spider.
Note: butterfly.
Note: necklace of flowers.
Note: dandelion.
[d̪ɾu̜ɫɑxɑṉ] Note: the cord passing under the two toes next to the big toe to keep the “osanan” in place.
[ɡɔɡʹɑṉ] Note: sort of knitted pixie with long tails which were crossed at the front and tied behind.
[kɔt̪əlʹĩ:ʃəɾiɡʹ] Note: coat for women and girls. Material: “ond” with linseed oil put on it.
Quot.: “cnèabailtean-beaga”. Note: garters put over trousers below the knee when going to the moor.
Note: echo.
Note: a grassy ledge on a cliff face; sheep may get stranded on one.
[ɡɤiʃiɡʹ] Note: jack snipe.
[t̪ɾı:lʹɑxɑṉ] Note: oystercatcher.
[cɛɾkçwʴsṯɑx] Note: fulmar (squirts oil). [NOTES: the turned r used for the symbol which is unclear in the original.]
[bɾıcəd̪] Quot.: Tha bricead ann. Note: noun from “breac” – speckled. Might also say “Tha nàdur bricich [bɾiciç] anns an aghaidh aige”.
Note: usually applied to a sheep’s face – dark but not quite black, perhaps little bits of grey among it.
Quot.: “caora chrosach”. Note: sheep with horns curving inwards towards the eyes.
Quot.: caora stàbhach. Note: a sheep with long wide horns.
Quot.: caora sgrogach. Note: a sheep with short curved horns, coming into the head.
Quot.: caora bhiorach. Note: a sheep with straight, pointed horns.
[ũ̟:s] Note: applied to the covering on a lamb’s fleece at birth.

[bɔ̃n̪ɑxhũ̟mɑṉɔx] Note: his pronunciation of “bonnach-iomanach”. A “bonnach” with plenty of “ùs” (cheese made with first milk) on it given as a reward to the first person to notice a cow was about to calf (leis a’ mhulad).
Note: drink made by pouring hot water on oatmeal.
[ʃtʹu̟:ɾɑɡ] Note: same as above [i.e. deoch-bhàn].
Note: a knock-out punch (blow).
Quot.: “Chuir e fuar e.” Note: He knocked him out.
Note: soapy water.
Note: water-brash.
[rwfɑṉiç] Note: broken skin behind fingernails.
Quot.: “Bhiodh uachdar nan troighean a’ gàgadh nuair a bhiodh daoine cas-ruisgt tràth air a bhliadhna.”
Note: ringworm. (Pl. buaileagan-timchioll.)
Quot.: “Sgeing e òrdag”. Note: He hit his toe and hurt it (e.g. on a stone when going barefoot). We would say also “Chuir e na sgeing e” – “He broke it beyond repair”.
Quot.: “mu chridhe an t-samhraidh”. Note: about the middle of summer.
Note: applied to a gland when it was swollen. Also: “Nuair a bha e a’ tionndadh bha e a’ fàgail fàireagan as a dheidh.” – bits of ground left unturned.
[fidʹiɡʹ] Quot.: “Gheibh thu mu na fidigean e.” Note: used mainly for hitting a person. Meant “about the legs”.
Note: àite beag, socair, blàth. Nest-like place.
[okɑx] Quot.: ochdach cléibh. Note: band round the chest when carrying a creel.
[ʃlʹɤɣɑɡ] Note: wooden spoon.
[bɑ:sd̪ɑð] Note: a soft boggy place with grass growing on it. Sheep would try to get at the grass and get stuck, or sink in it.
[bɔt̪] Note: deep hole on the moor, often dangerous because of overgrowing heather. (Pl. [bɔt̪əṉ].)
Note: “seorsa de bhreunlach [?] bhog agus feur gorm a’ fàs innte an cómhnaidh”; nas motha na bàsdair [q.v.]”.
Quot.: “a’ boidhteadh an dubhain”. Note: putting a worm on a fishing hook.
[bɔitʹɑṉ] Note: greiseag de dh’obair rudeigin cruaidh.
[bɔıtʹəɣ] Quot.: “a’ boiteadh dà rud ri chèile”. Note: fixing two things together – could be anything, wood, stone, yarn, etc.
[bɾe:dʹ] Quot.: “’S fheàrr bréid na toll.” Note: patch on clothing.

[kɔ̃nɔxkɑɡ] Quot.: “a’ seinn na conochdag”, “a’ séideadh na conochdag”. Note: a village horn was used in Bragar and Arnol until comparatively recently (prob. before the war) for a cessation of work outside. Could be for a death or before the weekly prayer-meeting or early on Saturday evening.
[ɑɫĩnʹ] Note: his pronunciation. Whisky and tobacco given out at a funeral. Did not see it himself. “Alainn an duine a bhasaich.”
Note: a bannock, of barley originally, with an egg mix put on top. (He said scrambled eggs.)
Quot.: “Chaidh a’ bhó ann am briach.” Note: getting stuck in a bog.
[t̪ɑfɔ̃nʹ] Quot.: “beathach ann an tabhoinn”. Note: a beast stuck in such a position that it cannot extricate itself.
Quot.: “atach caora”. Note: the remains of a dead sheep (just wool and bones).
Quot.: “closach caora”. Note: the dead body of a sheep.
Quot.: Bó a’ dol as a’ lasd. Note: dislocating the hip-joint.
[bɾɑlɑṉ] Note: the stomach of a sheep with flaps inside it.
[ĩtʹıɑx] Note: gullet.
[st̪ɤ̃ĩɡʹ] Note: “pìos feòil a ghearradh tu a beathach caorach.”
Quot.: beathach caorach, beathach mart. Note: a sheep, a cow.
Note: mixture of oatmeal and cold water. A stiffish mix.
Note: spinal marrow.
Note: applied to the jelly forming on cold veal.
Note: According to him it is “leabaidh a’ laoigh” in a calf [sic], but it is usually considered to be the stomach.
Quot.: “seann rosd”. Note: applied to an old person who is past the stage of being able to do anything. Also applied to an old animal in the same way.
Quot.: De an eileabanachd a th’ort a sin. Note: interfering or meddling with something one has no right to, e.g. a child up to mischief.
[sɡle:bəd̪ɑð] Note: applied to a person who would go into someone else’s house, eat his fill, and then go.
Note: applied to a woman who is always in and out of houses. (Also a’ siurraireachd.)
Quot.: “pìob buntàta”. Note: a pipe, the bowl of which was fashioned out of a potato, the stem being a length of the shaw. Used by boys for smoking “calcas”.
[rɑ̃n̪ɑ̃ṉ] Note: a jellyfish.
Quot.: sgeith a’ ròin. Note: jellyfish.
[ɡʹwbəṉɔx] Note: squid.
[rɔḏʃ] Quot.: roids de stoirm. Note: a fairly heavy storm – half-gale with a very rough sea.
[fɤ:viç] Quot.: “Tha an t-àite air fhaobhachadh.” Note: used in general of a place being cleaned out, e.g. a bay of fish.
[soɫɑʃ] Quot.: “Ghabh e sollais dheth.” Note: He ate a lot of it. Also: “Rinn e sollais air.” – He made a feast of it.
[t̪ɑ:vɔɾəɣ] Quot.: “Chunnaic mi a thàbhoradh.” Note: the ghost of a person – indicating that the person concerned was to die soon.

Quot.: “Theirig a dh’iarrraidh a’ nì.” Note: used formerly of cattle. Says that the form [nʹıç] was also used in certain instances. Not too clear about it but he thinks one would say “aig a’ nich”, “chon a’ nich”.
[ʃiɔɡɑṉ] Note: call to cattle in general.
[ʃtʹiɑɑɡ] Note: call to a cat.
[pɔıtʹi] Note: call to a pig.
[ˈɡlu̟ɑx] Note: applied to a fish in very poor condition.
Quot.: “gearranach math tapaidh”. Note: sometimes for “gearran” – a castrated stallion.
Note: miser.
[spi:kəðə] Note: miser.
[ɫomɑṉ] Quot.: “Lom ri loman agus lomaidh loman riut.” Note: give a little to a thrifty, tight person and you will get the same back.
[ʃtʹık] Note: when a person walks with one step shorter than the other due to a short leg. “Tha stioc ann” or “Tha stiocaich [ʃtʹikiç] ann”.
[ʃtʹıkəðə] Note: a person who walks with one step shorter than the other.
[ʃıkəðə] Quot.: Chaneil ann dheth ach siocaire grannda. Note: a person who is lazy, good for nothing but impertinent at the same time.
[ru̜ɤm] Quot.: “Tha ruam air.” “Ghabh e ruam” Note: a huff.
[splwɣəðə] Note: a tall, bony man.

[ȷu̜rɑm] Note: applied to the wailing of women formerly when a funeral cortege was leaving a house. “Ag iorram.” “An e so Uilleam, bhiodh e a’ falbh leis an iorram.” – local, said on meeting a dejected-looking person.
Quot.: cliath éisg. Note: a shoal of fish.
Quot.: siol a’ bhradain. Note: very young salmon in rivers before entering the sea. (Also siol a’ bhànaig.)
[ɡʹɔ:ləbɑṉ] Note: says it is the very young trout.
[ˈbɤidʹ] Quot.: “Tha baoghaid mhath air.” Note: a big belly.
Quot.: “port an daruis”. Note: when boys would start to get noisy in a céilidh house one might say “’S e port an daruis a th’agaibh a nis!” indicating they would have to leave.
[ɡɔɫɑɡ] Note: opening in a peat fire. “N a do shuidhe ris a’ ghollaig” also used.
Note: porpoise.
[ʃtʹwɾə] Note: a large type of dogfish.
Note: common sea bream.
Note: sturgeon. (Heard this but not local.)
